Job title: Assistant Professor of Economics - Environmental Economics and Sustainability

The Ketner School of Business at Catawba College (“Catawba”), ranked No. 1 among Regional Colleges in the South by U.S. News & World Report, welcomes applications for a tenure-track Assistant Professor of Economics, with a focus on environmental economics and sustainability, beginning August 2027. Ketner School of Business seeks a dynamic and engaged teacher-scholar who is passionate about undergraduate teaching, student mentorship, and program development and who is interested in applying economic analysis to environmental and sustainability challenges.

The school welcomes applicants whose teaching and research interests lie in environmental economics, natural resource economics, energy economics, climate economics, ecological economics, sustainable development, or related areas of applied economics. Particular areas of interest may include climate and energy policy, environmental and natural resource management, economic valuation, environmental markets, the economics of sustainability and decarbonization, sustainable development, and the economic dimensions of business and public-policy responses to environmental challenges. Ketner School of Business is particularly interested in candidates whose work complements Catawba’s institutional commitment to environmental education and sustainability and who value interdisciplinary collaboration and applied learning.

Candidates should hold a Ph.D. in Economics, Applied Economics, Environmental or Resource Economics, or a closely related field by the time of appointment. ABD candidates who expect to complete the doctorate before the start date will also be considered. Candidates should demonstrate the potential for excellence in undergraduate teaching and for an active program of scholarship appropriate to a teaching-centered liberal arts institution.

Primary responsibilities include excellence in teaching a range of economics courses at both the undergraduate and graduate levels. These will include foundational undergraduate courses such as Principles of Microeconomics and Principles of Macroeconomics, as well as upper-level courses in the candidate's areas of expertise. The successful candidate will also have opportunities to develop courses that strengthen Catawba's offerings in environmental and sustainability economics, including courses addressing topics such as environmental and natural resource economics, energy and climate economics, sustainable development, environmental policy, and market-based approaches to environmental challenges. Graduate teaching opportunities exist as well, including in the Ketner School's MBA program. Additional responsibilities include advising and mentoring students, engaging in scholarship, and contributing service to the Ketner School of Business and the College. The typical teaching load at Catawba College is 24 credit hours per academic year. Faculty also have opportunities to develop courses for Catawba's Honors Program and/or regularly offer a section of the First-Year Seminar as part of their teaching responsibilities.

The successful candidate will join a strategic cluster hire designed to embed environmental education and sustainability across Catawba College’s curriculum and co-curricular initiatives, becoming part of an interdisciplinary cohort of new campus thought leaders. As a member of this cohort, the faculty member will collaborate with colleagues across campus to strengthen students’ sustainability literacy, expand experiential learning, and utilize the campus, including its 189-acre ecological preserve, as a living learning laboratory. Together, the cohort will contribute to advancing Catawba’s mission as a leader in sustainability-driven higher education. Opportunities may also exist to contribute to interdisciplinary programs and initiatives spanning business, environmental studies, data science, public policy, and related fields.

Please find more info here.

Applicants must submit the following materials to econ26search@catawba.edu:

  • A letter of application;
  • Curriculum Vitae;
  • A statement of teaching philosophy (including evidence of teaching effectiveness, if available);
  • Evidence of scholarship (maximum of three examples); and
  • Contact information for three (3) professional references; references will not be contacted until candidates have successfully advanced through the initial stages of the selection process.

Review of completed applications begins on October 15, 2026, and continues until the position is filled.

Informal inquiries about the position should be directed to Dr. Eric Hake, Chair of the Search Committee, or to Dean Imran Chowdhury.

Job title: Lecturer - The Harry Van Arsdale Jr. School of Labor Studies

The Harry Van Arsdale Jr. School of Labor Studies at Empire State University (SUNY Empire) seeks to hire a lecturer based at its New York City location, where the majority of the Labor School's students attend face-to-face classes. The department invites candidates from a range of social science disciplines - including sociology, political science, anthropology, economics, and geography - with a commitment to participatory labor education and historical and/or contemporary research relevant to the labor movement, broadly defined to include unions, worker centers, and other social justice organizations.

The successful candidate will have expertise in Labor Studies and will teach, develop curriculum, and mentor/advise students in programs offered both in person and online. They will also design and develop high-quality online Labor Studies courses from existing curricula, working collaboratively with faculty and staff to translate course outcomes, readings, assignments, and assessments into engaging, accessible learning experiences within the university's learning management system. Central to the faculty role is helping adults from diverse cultural backgrounds design and complete degrees that meet their personal and professional goals. SUNY Empire faculty provide advising from entry through graduation to students in the Labor Studies academic program. Working in cooperation with faculty and staff, the successful candidate will provide high-quality educational services to students, pursue relevant scholarly interests, participate in University life, and enhance the University and HVASLS's reputation and impact within the community.

The Harry Van Arsdale Jr. School of Labor Studies (HVASLS) is one of the founding programs of Empire State University. It currently serves approximately 1,000 students through partnerships with various labor organizations in New York City, and it offers in-person, as well as online and residency programs to members of partner organizations from across the country. Its labor-centered liberal arts program was inspired by Harry Van Arsdale Jr., a major twentieth century labor leader and a tireless promoter of life-long education for members of his union, IBEW Local 3, and all working people.

The Van Arsdale program offers associate and bachelor's degrees in Labor Studies as well as non-degree certificate programs. The program seeks to build a broad and inclusive labor and community-centered approach to help develop solutions to the most pressing challenges that our society is facing today, including issues related to economic, racial, and gender inequalities, globalization, technological change, industrial and financial restructuring. The courses are designed to provide the knowledge, awareness, and skills needed for our students to become leaders in the labor movement and in their communities.

Required Qualifications:

  • Master's degree in labor studies or related social science disciplines such as sociology, political science, anthropology, economics, and geography.
  • Demonstrated experience designing, developing, and teaching online courses in a learning management system, including building courses from existing curricula, organizing course content, developing learning activities and assessments, and supporting student engagement in an online environment.
  • Experience with labor education, the labor movement, and social justice movements.
  • College-level teaching experience.
  • Experience teaching and/or advising non-traditional students from diverse backgrounds.

Preferred Qualifications:

  • PhD. in Labor Studies, or related social science disciplines such as sociology, political science, anthropology, economics, and geography.
  • Experience teaching courses in Labor Studies or courses on labor topics in related fields.
  • Demonstrated commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion in higher education and/or through community-based work.
  • Demonstrated commitment to a participatory pedagogy.
  • Research interests in issues related to working people, labor organizations, and social movements.
  • Familiarity with the D2L Brightspace learning management system.

Special Information:

  • Candidates should include with their application a statement on their teaching philosophy and methods.
  • Occasional travel will be required to fulfill university-wide obligations, including biannual travel to Saratoga Springs, New York.
  • Office hours will vary in accordance with student needs. Periodic evening and weekend engagement will also be required.
  • Applicants must be currently authorized to work in the U.S. on a full-time basis. VISA sponsorship is not available for this position.
  • SUNY Empire provides employees with robust remote and flexible work options to meet the needs of students, faculty, and staff in a dispersed work environment.

On the other hand, the department investigates how societies deal with the increasing transformation requirements of the global climate and biodiversity crisis (newer transformation sociology). Job title: Clinical Assistant Professor - Economics

Liberal Studies at New York University invites applications for a Clinical Assistant Professor position to begin September 1, 2027, pending administrative and budgetary approval. The Liberal Studies Core is a dynamic liberal arts curriculum that provides a global and interdisciplinary foundation for nearly 100 NYU majors. The Global Liberal Studies Bachelor of Arts is an innovative global studies major grounded in the spatial, conceptual, and temporal understandings of a highly interconnected world, with a program of study that is distinguished by experiential learning, study away, and independent research focused in an interdisciplinary concentration. In both the LS Core and the GLS major, small, seminar-style classes and close faculty-student interaction provide students with the benefits of a liberal arts college within a large urban research university. The coordinators are especially interested in hiring qualified candidates who can contribute their research, teaching, and service to the diversity and excellence of Liberal Studies and NYU.

Candidates should be able to teach introductory microeconomics and macroeconomics in a liberal arts context from both mainstream and heterodox perspectives. The coordinators seek colleagues who, as needed, will teach intermediate and advanced courses in the listed fields of specialization in the Economy and Society Concentration (E&S) of Global Liberal Studies. Candidates should emphasize interdisciplinary and global connections in their teaching and research. They must apply theoretical analysis to real-world events in lectures and show a commitment to fostering an inclusive, collegial classroom environment.

Minimum qualifications: PhD by the date of appointment; three years of college-level teaching experience; and demonstrated excellence in teaching. The coordinators are especially interested in qualified candidates who share Liberal Studies’ commitment to equity, inclusion, and belonging, and who can contribute to the diversity of intellectual life in LS and NYU. Candidates must present demonstrated experience and commitment to interdisciplinarity, intersectionality, and a teaching approach informed by global perspectives. Publications and evidence of outstanding scholarship and relevant professional activity are strongly encouraged.

All Liberal Studies full-time faculty hold renewable term contracts, initially three years, and later six years in duration. Faculty are eligible for promotion within the Clinical faculty ranks (Assistant, Associate, Full). Faculty normally teach three classes per semester, advise undergraduates, and contribute service to Liberal Studies and to the University. In compliance with NYC’s Pay Transparency Act, the annual base salary for this position is $93,730. New York University considers factors such as (but not limited to) the scope and responsibilities of the position, the candidate’s work experience, education/training, key skills, internal peer equity, as well as market and organizational considerations when extending an offer.

Applications include ONLY (1) a cover letter and (2) a current CV. Complete applications must be recorded by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (US), November 22, 2026. Applications recorded after this deadline will not be considered.

You want to understand how things are connected and make a fundamental impact? The institute for Economic and Social History offers an environment where you can realize your full potential. At one of Europe’s largest and most modern business and economics universities. On a campus where quality of work is also quality of life.

Pursuant to WU’s Personnel Development Plan, this position can only be fixed-term for up to six years. Once all objectives agreed upon in the qualification agreement have been fulfilled, the employment relationship can be made permanent. Employees who have successfully completed a qualification agreement are classified as associate professors. From an organizational regulation perspective they belong to the group of professors. Three years after successful completion of the qualification agreement, they are entitled to apply for promotion to full professor according to the By-Laws of WU § 43a.

The institute is inviting applications for an Assistant Professor position (tenure track) in the field of Economic History to join our institute. This tenure track assistant professor position offers the opportunity to advance an independent research profile, publish internationally, acquire funding and gain substantial teaching experience while working collaboratively within a close-knit group of colleagues who share a strong interest in the field. Deadline: 9 November 2026

Job title: Post Doctoral Research Associate in Agent-Based Climate Macroeconomics

The University of Oxford is seeking a Postdoctoral Research Associate to contribute to research examining the macroeconomic impacts of UK climate mitigation policies. Based at the Institute for New Economic Thinking (INET), the successful candidate will join the MacroCB7 – Macroeconomics of the Seventh Carbon Budget project, working closely with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) to assess how climate policies affect economic growth, employment, inflation and inequality.

Working with Professor Doyne Farmer, Tom Youngman and Dr. Donal Brown, you will contribute to the development and application of an innovative agent-based macroeconomic model to evaluate the economic and distributional consequences of net zero policies. Research will explore areas including low-carbon heating technologies, government finances, alternative investment scenarios and the potential for social tipping points in climate transitions.

The role combines quantitative research, software development and policy engagement. You will develop and implement new modelling approaches using Python, analyse esults through sensitivity testing and simulation, contribute to academic publications, and present findings to government and policy partners. From June 2027, the research will expand to examine transformative net zero policies across energy, housing, transport and food, with a particular focus on reducing inequality alongside greenhouse gas emissions.

The University of Oxford is seeking candidates who hold, or are close to completion of, a PhD/DPhil in a relevant discipline, with programming experience and a strong understanding of economic theory, particularly macroeconomics and complexity approaches. You should have excellent analytical and communication skills, experience contributing to research publications, and an interest in applying quantitative modelling to climate policy. Experience in agent-based modelling, collaborative coding or policy-engaged research would be advantageous.

The role is based at INET's offices on Manor Road, Oxford. Flexible working arrangements may be considered, subject to discussion and approval, including part-time working at 0.5 FTE or above. A minimum of one day per week in the office during term time is expected.

This position offers the opportunity to develop and apply innovative economic modelling methods to inform UK climate policy, working within an interdisciplinary research team with established government partnerships. This post is offered on a full-time, fixed-term basis for 18 months upon start date. (Part-time arrangements of 0.5 FTE or above may be considered)

Deadline: 15 November 2026

Job title: Assistant Professor in Economics

The Utrecht University School of Economics (U.S.E.) invites applications for an Assistant Professor position in Economics. The position is embedded in the Applied Economics section.

The Applied Economics section brings together researchers working in a large variety of areas of applied economics (e.g. public economics, behavioral economics, health economics, economics of crime, regional/urban economics, development economics, labour economics, economics of education, and other applied fields) with researchers working on the history, methodology, and/or philosophy of economics. Research and teaching in the section is typically empirical, policy-oriented, and sometimes multidisciplinary.

The position involves teaching in areas where economics is itself the object of study. These areas include the history of economics, economic history, philosophy of economics, and economic/econometric methodology, such as for example the courses “Contemporary Economics in Historical Perspectives” or “Ethical and Historical Reflections”. Candidates should explain in their cover letter how their research connects to these teaching areas.

The position includes 60% teaching time (including 5% governance), and 40% research time.

The candidate’s responsibilities will include:

  • conducting high-quality research in economics or a closely related field;
  • teaching undergraduate and graduate courses within U.S.E.;
  • contributing to courses at U.S.E. in which economics is reflected upon (e.g. history of economic thought, philosophy of economics, economic methodology, or related themes) but also teach at the Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) programme to which U.S.E. contributes;

The Institute for Ecological Economics is looking for a post-doctoral researcher in climate and nature finance, with a focus and interest on their international development aspects. The position is based at the Institute for Ecological Economics, within the Vienna University of Economics and Business, under the supervision of Irene Monasterolo. You will work with the experts of the Task Force on Climate, Development and the International Financial Architecture led by Boston University in collaboration with the G24 and V20 on reshaping international climate finance for development, in dialogue with multinational development banks and financial institutions.

Within the project, you will contribute to inform how different financial arrangements and instruments could contribute to build resilience to climate and nature risks, in an inclusive and financial stability-aware way. You will explore the conditions for climate development finance to act a global shock absorber in the context of climate and nature risks. In particular, you will provide new conceptual and quantitative insights on debt, financial instruments and measures (e.g. Resilience and Sustainability Facility, Recovery and Resilience Facility, Capital Flow Management Measures, Regional Financing Arrangements, equity), including a global insurance scheme, for emerging markets and low-income economies (EMDEs). This is a crucial topic for the future of international development: growing socio-economic losses from climate change and ecosystem depletion, and geopolitical instability, contribute to decrease countries’ fiscal space and to increase the cost of investing in resilience. In this context, EMDEs face a future of sluggish development, insufficient resilience and sustainability, and new debt crises, with cascading effects on the economy of Global North countries. You will work in close contact with a team of experts in climate finance for development with long experience in development finance institutions. You will have the opportunity to attend international research and policy workshops, conferences, and have policy impact, shaping the discussion about the international climate finance agenda.

Job title: PhD Opportunity in Energy and Disaster Risk Management

Project description:

There is growing demand to explore the potential linkage between SDG-7 (which emphasises energy) and SDG-13 (which emphasises climate actions). In this context, the primary goal is to develop a conceptual link between access to energy and climate adaptation. Researchers have claimed that access to energy is a critical enabler for development. It is also important to see the relationship between access to energy and development practices. Researchers claimed that appropriate integration of energy works as a catalyst for rural development activities (Gevelt et al., 2018). But it is not clear how energy influences climate adaptation capacities and development outcomes. The role of the modern energy system has been given emphasis for post-disaster recovery and reconstruction globally. The access to energy becomes crucial for increasing climate threats on vulnerable communities in the world. It is also established that development planning and practices are influenced by the positive outcome of access to energy and climate adaptation efforts. Electricity supply is very essential in disaster affected areas to fulfil the services during an emergency. Studies have found that coastal regions are highly prone to saline water flooding and cyclones due to climate change (Hoque et al.,2019). The hydro-climatic natural hazards often affect the electric supply and therefore, disaster mitigation measures are affected. Solar power is one of the most reliable sources of energy when traditional power grids are susceptible to damage during disasters. Solar energy infrastructures operate individually and generate power when the main grid fails and provide a stable supply of energy. Solar power becomes an ideal off-grid solution in disaster affected areas having limited sources of conventional energy. Solar power becomes essential for emergency shelters, providing emergency health and communication services. As per Scott et al., (2017) solar energy based power supply increase the three core resilience capacities namely anticipatory, adaptive and absorptive capacities of vulnerabilities people in rural areas. Therefore, the present mixed methdological research will explore how solar energy contribute to the lives and livelihood of people living with disasters. The study will analyse how the solar energy resource contribute coping mechanism of households after disaster.

This work offers:

  • A joint PhD award from BITS Pilani, India and RMIT University, Australia
  • Full tuition scholarships from RMIT and highly subsidised fees at BITS

Job title: Researcher in History in project on families and inheritance

The position is based at the Department of History, Lund University, and forms part of a larger research project involving two principal investigators and a student research assistant. Most of the work will be carried out at the department, although occasional work may also take place at archival institutions elsewhere in Sweden. One of the project members is based abroad, which means that project meetings will be held both in person in Lund and online.

The GeneaLogies of Old Wealth (GLOW) research project is a multi-year project funded by the Swedish Research Council (Vetenskapsrådet). It examines wealthy families and analyses the significance of inherited wealth across multiple generations. Using Sweden's wealthiest families at the beginning of the twentieth century as its point of departure, the project has reconstructed their economic trajectories by combining four-generation family trees with financial information derived from probate inventories.

The main phase of data collection has now been completed, and the project is entering a stage of data processing, analysis, and writing. The project offers new perspectives on historical economic inequality, a major field of research both in Sweden and internationally. GLOW forms part of the research node HEIRS at the Department of History, which specialises in research on household economies, wealth, and inheritance.

The successful candidate will be expected to:

  • Process and analyse the collected source material.
  • Author two scholarly articles within the framework of the project, one co-authored and one single-authored.
  • Present the project and its research findings at academic conferences.
  • Develop ways of disseminating the project's results to wider audiences, for example through blog posts, newspaper articles, or other forms of public engagement.
  • Contribute actively to the development of the HEIRS research node and its activities.
  • Contribute to the development of new research grant applications associated with HEIRS.

As a researcher in the project, you are expected to work independently while maintaining close and continuous collaboration with the other members of the research team. Although your work will be carried out within the overall framework of the project, you will have considerable scope to shape the direction of your analyses, particularly in relation to the single-authored article. This article should be based on the project's data, but its thematic focus may be developed in line with your own expertise and research interests.

Required Qualifications

PhD position - '(Dis)orderly transitions: The financial sector's role in shaping just energy transitions'

What the project is about

In recent years the idea of an 'orderly just transition' has started to gain ground. While questions of justice have been taken up by ‘just transition’ research, the addition of 'orderly' is more recent, raising new questions around the envisioned speed, direction, and outcomes of energy transitions. In this project we want to look at this idea of 'order' in transitions more closely, identifying and analysing how (some) actors in the financial sector try to implement an orderly transition away from fossil fuels through the use of specific financial instruments and practices. By incorporating ideas from both political economy and economic sociology the project investigates how attempts at enacting order by financial actors can be understood as a process of contested temporal politics, with actors seeking to make the future knowable, trajectories towards it manageable, and outcomes controllable.

Who you will be working with

The project is a collaboration between myself (Bregje van Veelen, Lund University) and Amy Janzwood at McGill University in Canada, and will include cases in both North America and Scandinavia. The PhD candidate in Lund is expected to focus primarily on the latter, but there will be opportunity for comparative work too. The position is based at LUCSUS (Lund University Centre for Sustainability Studies) in Sweden, where you will be part of a friendly and supportive community of scholars.

What the institution is looking for in a candidate

Someone with a strong interest in critical social science approaches who is excited to explore how issues of politics and power play out in the financial sphere. The project speaks to a variety of themes and concepts, including energy transitions, sustainable finance, temporalities & future-making, and social constructions of risk. The institution does not expect anyone to be experienced with all of these, but having experience with one of these topics and an interest in some of the others is important. Most of the data collection is expected to be qualitative in nature, so experience with qualitative methods is a must. Knowledge of a Scandinavian language is a bonus, but not a requirement.

For potential applicants unfamiliar with the Swedish system

PhD positions in Sweden are fully funded for 4 years. The project examines the transformation of global financial structures in the context of increasing geopolitical tensions and analyzes China’s efforts to build an alternative, Sinocentric financial system. It focuses on processes of policy learning, the emergence of imperial practices, and their role in reshaping global patterns of power, autonomy, and dependence.

Autonomy, Dependence, and China’s Emerging Imperial Practices” (FOR 5913/1), a large collaborative initiative to study China's changing international practices under the conditions of a world order in transition funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG). Supporting early-career researchers is a central priority of the “Learning Empire” Research Unit. The program emphasizes the development of transferable academic skills, research practices, and integration into the group’s shared intellectual and methodological framework. This is complemented by a dedicated workshop program, writing retreats, and active participation in collaborative events, fostering both professional development and a strong interdisciplinary research community.

Job Title: Doctoral student in Economic History

We are pleased to share that the Department of Economic History at Lund University is currently inviting applications for two PhD positions: Greenspace Across the Life Course: Inequality, School Outcomes, and Later Health

The aim of the project is to investigate, from a life-course perspective, how exposure to greenspace around the home, at school, along routes to and from school and work, and at the workplace is associated with social inequality, school outcomes, and later-life health. The project combines historical microdata for Landskrona, 1892–1967, geocoded at the block and address levels, with modern geocoded Swedish register data, 1968–2023, and high-resolution geospatial data. Using historical maps, orthophotos, and satellite imagery, the project develops measures of greenspace over time, which are then analysed using quantitative longitudinal and spatial methods.

The PhD student will contribute to the empirical and methodological development of the project, for example, through research on inequality in access to greenspace, the relationship between greenspace and school outcomes in both historical and modern periods, and the long-term relationship between childhood environments and later-life health. The project is interdisciplinary but clearly rooted in economic history through its focus on long-term processes, inequality, education, and health.

Job title: Postdoctoral Position in the project "Immigration and Ideological Activation in the Second Spanish Republic: Crisis, Mobilization, and Political Integration

The Department of Economic History, Institutions, Politics and World Economy at the University of Barcelona (UB) and the Institutions and Political Economy Research Group (IPERG) invite applications for a Postdoctoral Position in the project "Immigration and Ideological Activation in the Second Spanish Republic: Crisis, Mobilization, and Political Integration," led by Francesc Amat and funded by the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities (Consolidación Investigadora 2025, CNS2025-166672). The project investigates how immigrants in Barcelona during the Second Spanish Republic (1930s) became politically activated and integrated, despite cultural, educational, and economic disadvantages. Its central hypothesis focuses on horizontal ideological transmission—how political ideas and behaviors spread peer-to-peer—as a key mechanism of political socialization.

About the position: The successful candidate will become a member of the project's research team and collaborate closely with the PI. The Postdoctoral fellow is expected to:

  • Co-author working papers and academic articles related to the project together with the PI.
  • Contribute to the development of the project, particularly with data collection, digitization, and quantitative analysis of historical sources.
  • Participate in and contribute to the organization of the project's conferences, seminars, and workshops.

We offer a 1-year full-time Postdoctoral Position, with the possibility of an extension—subject to approval by the PI and depending on funding constraints. The position includes additional funding for conference travel, methods training, and research stays. The annual gross salary is in the range of €35,000–40,000.

Within the framework of three thematic clusters (Ecosystem Dynamics, Human activities and Governance), ECORISK deals with the causes of ecological regime shifts and the systemic risks they pose as well as their consequences in socio-ecological systems.
Intensive agriculture serves as a guiding example. The Research Training Group is located at Osnabrück University, whose diverse research attracts students and scholars from around the world to a liveable city.

In the subproject "Participatory Interventions to Foster Cooperation in the Face of Regime Shifts and Systemic Risk" at the Department of Environmental Economics in the School of Business Administration and Economics, a position as Research Assistant / PhD Candidate.

Specifically, the work would focus on a) contributing to the review of relevant streams of literature on participatory governance arrangements/capacities to overcome collective action challenges among heterogenous stakeholders; b) designing a suitable participatory intervention to bridge (perceived) distance and promote collective action (skills) among heterogenous stakeholders in the context of sustainable agriculture or food systems; and c) assessing the potential of the selected intervention, e.g. through an economic field experiment or a before-and-after impact assessment.

  • Strong research interest in the (participatory) processes that can generate (the capacities for) inner change for sustainability transformation at the individual and the societal level (for ex. a change in perceptions of social distance/norms, trust, or empathic concern)
  • Very good English language skills in both spoken and written form
